edits.english: The court issued a ruling - And the majority of the public acted according to their ruling:
And they discovered that they erred and reversed their decision - from their ruling:

Whether they brought their atonement offering or whether they did not bring their atonement offering - And after they knew that they erred, the individual went and acted according to their ruling, for this does not combine with the majority of the public, because this individual acted after it became known to them:

Rabbi Shimon deems him exempt - Because he acts with the permission of the court, as this individual still did not know that they (the court) erred and reversed their decision, and he is considered to be relying on the court. Therefore, he is exempt:
Rabbi Elazar says: Uncertainty - Meaning, it is uncertain whether he is considered to be relying on the court or relying on himself, and he brings a provisional guilt-offering:
Which is the case of uncertainty - Meaning, why is he liable to bring a provisional guilt-offering:
If one sat inside his house he is liable - to bring a provisional guilt-offering:

MISHNA: The court issued an erroneous ruling, and they discovered that they erred and reversed their decision, whether they brought their atonement (offering) for what they ruled or whether they did not bring their atonement, and a person who did not know that they reversed their decision proceeded and performed a transgression on the basis of their ruling — Rabbi Shimon deems him exempt from an offering, and Rabbi Elazar says: It is uncertainty, and he brings a provisional guilt-offering. Which is the case of uncertainty? When is something considered an uncertainty for which one is liable to bring a provisional guilt-offering? If a person sat inside his house and did so — he is liable to bring a guilt-offering, as he could have known that the court reversed its decision. If he went to a country overseas and is still relying on the old ruling — he is exempt.

And here it is discussed when the majority of the public acted according to the court's ruling (Rashi). Indeed, the Meiri believes that what emerges from this Mishnah is that it is based on the reasoning that an individual who acted according to the court's ruling is exempt, and not only the first Tanna but also the other Tannaim agree in principle with this view. And he noted that this is the reasoning, even though there is seemingly a contradiction from Tractate Shabbat. And indeed, in Tosafot there (93b), they raised a difficulty from here on Rashi's words there, where Rabbi Shimon holds that an individual who acted according to the court's ruling is liable. However, from Rashi's language here, it can be understood that it refers to an individual who acted in conjunction with the entire public (and see the words of the commentators).

Meaning, in which case do we have uncertainty whether his status is considered as relying on the court or not (Rabbi Yonatan). And later commentators noted that Rashi's words should also be understood this way.

The court issued a ruling and erred, and afterwards they reversed their decision. And an individual performed an action according to their ruling after their error became known to them — this person brings a provisional guilt-offering. Since he could have asked if anything new had occurred in the court but did not ask, he is like one who is uncertain if he committed a transgression. But if he traveled to a country overseas, even if he performed the action after the error became known to the court — he is exempt, because he relied on them, and it was impossible for him to ask. This is in accordance with the words of Rabbi Elazar, to whom Rabbi Akiva also concedes. (Rambam Sefer Korbanot, Hilkhot Shegagot 14:5).

A court that erred and ruled to abolish an entire category of Torah law, even if the entire congregation acted according to their ruling — the court is exempt, and each individual who performed the action is liable to bring a sin-offering. This is like an unstated Mishnah. (Rambam Sefer Korbanot, Hilkhot Shegagot 14:1).
That he is closer to exemption - For he is certainly considered to be relying on the court, as he did not know of their reversal, since he went to a country overseas:
Ben Azzai said to him: In what way is this different - The one who went to a country overseas, from one who sits in his house:

Rabbi Akiva said to him - Because one who sits in his house could possibly hear that the court reversed its decision, and is therefore close to being considered as relying on himself, and is consequently liable to bring a provisional guilt-offering. But this one who went to a country overseas could not hear, and is truly considered to be relying on the court. Therefore, he is exempt:

Rabbi Akiva said: I concede in that case of one who went to a country overseas that he is closer to exemption than to liability. Ben Azzai said to him: In what way is this person different from one who sits in his house? He said to him: That one who sits in his house it would have been possible for him to hear, but this one who is in a country overseas it would not have been possible for him to hear. And from here the Mishnah comes to explain in what matter the thing is considered an erroneous ruling for which the public brings an offering.

The Rosh wonders: The essence of this view is from the words of the Tanna Rabbi Elazar (ben Shamua), who was a student of Rabbi Akiva (and according to the names of the disputing Tannaim, it is clear that it is impossible to read 'Rabbi Eliezer' here), and it is puzzling that Rabbi Akiva would use this language of concession regarding the words of his student. Indeed, the commentators have already brought the version of the Yerushalmi (according to an old reading) where it says "I see" in this place, and this language is appropriate even in the words of a teacher regarding his student (Magen Giborim, Ḥok Natan).

The mishna explains for which type of unwitting transgression based on the ruling of the court there is liability to bring an offering. In a case where the judges of the court issued an erroneous ruling to abolish the entire essence of a mitzva, not only a detail thereof, e.g., they said: There is no prohibition against engaging in intercourse with a menstruating woman written in the Torah, or there is no prohibition against performing prohibited labor on Shabbat written in the Torah, or there is no prohibition against engaging in idol worship written in the Torah, these judges are exempt, as this is an error based on ignorance, not an erroneous ruling. If the judges issued a ruling to nullify part of a mitzva and to sustain part of that mitzva, these judges are liable.

The court issued a ruling to abolish the entire essence of the mitzvah and not a single detail from it, for example, if they said: There is no prohibition against engaging in intercourse with a menstruating woman written in the Torah, there is no prohibition against performing prohibited labor on Shabbat written in the Torah, there is no prohibition against engaging in idol worship written in the Torah — these judges are exempt. For this is not an erroneous ruling but a simple mistake. If they issued a ruling to nullify part of the mitzvah and to sustain part of it — these judges are liable.

A court is never liable unless it issued a ruling to nullify part and sustain part in matters that are not explicitly stated in the Torah. For example, if they erred and said that carrying from one domain to another on Shabbat is prohibited, but passing an object is permitted, or if they said that bowing to an idol without extending one's hands and feet is permitted. This is like an unstated Mishnah and its explanation will be given later in the Gemara. (Rambam Sefer Korbanot, Hilkhot Shegagot 14:2).

How so? An example of this is if the judges said: There is a prohibition against engaging in intercourse with a menstruating woman written in the Torah, but one who engages in intercourse with a woman who observes a clean day for a day she experiences a discharge is exempt. When the woman sees a discharge of blood for one or two days during the eleven days between the end of one menstrual period and the expected start of another, the blood is assumed to not be menstrual blood. If after the second day, the next day passes without any discharge of blood, she may immerse immediately and she is ritually pure. The judges ruled erroneously that it is permitted to engage in intercourse with her on the day that she is observing a clean day, even without the day having passed and her having immersed; or if they said:

How so? If they said: There is a prohibition against engaging in intercourse with a menstruating woman written in the Torah, but one who engages in intercourse with a woman who observes a day for a day — referring to a woman who saw menstrual blood not at its regular time for one day, in which case she needs to observe a second day and check if her menstruation continues, and even if she did not see blood on the second day, she is considered a menstruating woman for that day — and they ruled that one who engages in intercourse with her is exempt, or if they said:
There is Shabbat in the Torah, but one who carries out from the private domain to the public domain is exempt.

There is idol worship in the Torah, but one who bows (who did not offer a sacrifice to it) is exempt — these judges are liable for an erroneous ruling, as it is stated: “And the matter is hidden” (Leviticus 4:13), to say “a matter” — a single detail, and not the entire essence.
